channel.title: Noticias del Mundo — Ciencia
channel.description: Noticias de ciencia de todas las fuentes configuradas.

item.title: Bowen pushes pragmatic climate deal amid pressure over fossil fuels
item.description: Chris Bowen says Australia's coal and gas exports have not damaged its standing in climate negotiations, as countries struggle to agree on how to move away from fossil fuels. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: How human ideas evolve: Technical progress may not require weeding out weaker designs
item.description: Human culture evolves similarly to living organisms, but unlike biology, human creativity can accumulate improvements at an incredible speed. But how exactly does the process of transmitting and modifying ideas between people work? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Space dust particles point to ancient heavy-oxygen water reservoir in the Kuiper belt
item.description: Way out past the asteroid belt, another belt encircles the planets in our solar system. The Kuiper belt, beyond Neptune, preserves icy bodies that escaped much of the processing experienced by objects closer to the sun. Unlike the rocky and metallic asteroid belt, Kuiper belt objects are composed mostly of frozen water, methane and ammonia, mixed with rock and dust. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Building a rocket is hard. AST SpaceMobile thinks it's "simple."
item.description: "We're not doing this thing because we like rockets." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: Transparency in earnings calls does not guarantee equal access to information
item.description: The specialized language used by analysts and management in listed companies' Q&A sessions can be challenging for individual investors to follow. However, Kaisa Penttinen's doctoral dissertation in accounting at the University of Vaasa, Finland, shows these sessions still deliver useful information beyond what is disclosed in written reports alone. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A rare star system emits radio signals every 8 minutes
item.description: Scientists at the Curtin University node at the International Center for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) have linked mysterious radio pulses to an unusual pairing of stars—a dead star that spins every eight minutes and a star similar to our own sun. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How the discovery of a Roman fort rekindled interest in an emperor immortalized in Welsh mythology
item.description: The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, southwest Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A living shield: Skin microbes may help sawfish survive oxygen-poor pools
item.description: This large freshwater sawfish might look scary, but its greatest survival assets are tiny microbes that may give its young an invisible force field when environmental conditions get tough. New research led by Flinders University describes how microscopic communities living on the skin of the critically endangered largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) could help these animals endure challenging dry-season conditions, offering a new perspective on their conservation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lemon waste yields bioplastic more flexible than commercial counterpart, study finds
item.description: A new research article published in Polymers explores an innovative way to turn lemon processing residues into biopolymers. Authored by ANIPH's coordinator, CETEC, together with partners from companion projects Viss and PHAntastic, the study investigated the use of lemon industry byproducts as carbon sources for PHBV production using the halophilic archaeon Haloferax mediterranei. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Ames Stars of the Month: November 2026
item.description: The NASA Ames Science Directorate recognizes the outstanding contributions of (pictured left to right) Alyssa Villanueva, Steve Howell, and Samuel LeBlanc. Their commitment to the NASA mission represents the entrepreneurial spirit, technical expertise, and collaborative disposition needed to explore this world and beyond. Space Biosciences Star: Alyssa Villanueva Alyssa Villaneuva is an engineer at Blue […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Aaron McKinnon

item.title: Liquid-phase growth strategy densifies ceramic films at low temperature
item.description: Ceramic films are widely used in solid-state batteries, energy conversion devices and electronic systems. Their fabrication, however, often requires high-temperature sintering, which can cause elemental volatilization, compositional segregation and undesirable interfacial reactions. Achieving dense, compositionally uniform ceramic films at lower temperatures therefore remains a challenge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new view of the gamma-ray gap: 14 years of Fermi data reveal around 450 sources in a largely unexplored energy range
item.description: The universe is filled with light at many different energies. Some of it is invisible to our eyes, including extremely energetic gamma rays, which can only be produced in the most extreme environments in our universe, for example supermassive black holes, exploding stars or astrophysical jets. To "see" gamma rays, astrophysicists use particle experiments in space, such as the Fermi-Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT). This instrument was launched into space by NASA in 2008, and it can detect photons from 20 megaelectronvolts (MeV, a unit of energy) to beyond 1 teraelectronvolt (TeV). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A suspected black hole turns out to be a rapidly spinning star
item.description: Sometimes massive stars can mimic the behavior of a black hole and trick astronomers into misinterpreting their nature. Such is the case with a strange pair of stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) cluster NGC 1850. The system was initially thought to contain a star about five times the mass of the sun orbiting a stellar-mass black hole. Now, a new study led by Rhys Seeburger of Liverpool John Moores University demonstrates that this is a black hole "impostor" system. The research paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 27. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Pumpkin seed protein puts a twist on nondairy coffee creamer
item.description: Pumpkin season is about more than cute décor. The squash contains lots of seeds with a high protein content, but they're usually discarded. Researchers reporting in ACS' Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry found another way to use the seeds, extracting that protein to create a plant-based coffee creamer. In initial taste tests, participants preferred the new creamer to a commercial nondairy option because it preserved the flavor and aroma of coffee better. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Simulated collisions reveal how Phobos could preserve rocks blasted off Mars
item.description: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, but their origins remain uncertain. Were they asteroids captured by Mars' gravity, or did they form from debris following a giant impact on the planet? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sequential peaks in arthropod availability across snow and vegetation help sustain alpine birds
item.description: The alpine zone is located above the tree line in mountainous regions and is characterized by long winters and short growing seasons. Birds and other animals inhabiting these environments breed during a limited period extending from spring to summer. Arthropods, including insects and spiders, serve as an essential food resource during this time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Finding romance with AI: Study explores benefits, limits of chatbot intimacy
item.description: An AI companion can be available for a late-night conversation, respond to personal disclosures and discuss a favorite topic for hours. For people who develop intimate relationships with chatbots, those exchanges can offer a meaningful sense of connection. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds
item.description: Shoppers using AI chatbots to research products or find places to buy items could be directed to imposters and other risky websites, a new study found. The study conducted by IP protection firm Podqi and shared exclusively with The Verge prompted ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity with a handful of shopping-related questions involving a selection of […] Fuente: The Verge.
item.dc:creator: Mia Sato

item.title: Lipids from banana peels help cherry tomatoes stay fresh longer
item.description: Fruits and vegetables keep "breathing" even after they're picked. Respiration consumes sugars and organic acids that contribute to flavor, while moisture loss and continued ripening soften the fruit. These changes shorten shelf life and contribute to food waste. Thin edible coatings can be applied to regulate gas and water transfer and preserve fresh produce. Now, food scientists are exploring whether byproducts we often discard could supply ingredients for these coatings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New analytical method offers potential for faster risk assessment of avian influenza viruses
item.description: Highly pathogenic avian influenza causes significant damage to the poultry industry worldwide. As the virus evolves, new variants regularly emerge that may differ in how easily they spread and how severely they affect infected birds. Researchers at Wageningen Bioveterinary Research (WBVR, part of Wageningen University & Research) characterized eight avian influenza virus variants in chicken and duck cells. Using mathematical modeling, they identified differences in how these viruses behave in poultry cells. Their paper is published in Microbiology Spectrum. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny cracks and a 9-volt battery could help fight deadly superbugs
item.description: As superbugs become harder to treat and antibiotic resistance continues to rise worldwide, Flinders University scientists have uncovered an unlikely ally in the fight to prevent infections before they take hold. They have found that carefully controlled microscopic cracks can enhance the performance of an antibacterial coating, which helps destroy dangerous bacteria when activated with a small electrical charge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Feeling pressured to be grateful? Don't force it
item.description: It's that time of year when gratitude seems to be everywhere: at work, around the dinner table and at holiday gatherings. But with so much pressure to feel thankful, gratitude can start to feel like one more thing on the holiday to-do list. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rain may increase ocean carbon uptake more than we thought
item.description: Global carbon budgets, which track carbon's movement among the atmosphere, ocean and land, may underestimate how much carbon the ocean absorbs by roughly 5% to 15% because current estimates do not fully account for rain's effects on the ocean surface. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unified framework establishes rules for classifying unconventional magnets
item.description: Researchers from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science (HFIPS) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) have developed a unified framework for establishing symmetry criteria and classifying unconventional magnets. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds midlife women face unique need for workplace flexibility
item.description: New research from the Working for Women Research Partnership (WFWRP) shows overlapping life demands make women ages 40–55 more likely than other groups to both want and need workplace flexibility. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: "Actuar por Francia": las escalofriantes declaraciones del autor del atentado racista de Trappes
item.description: Kévin Tessier, principal sospechoso del ataque racista del 23 de octubre en el departamento de Yvelines, hizo revelaciones estremecedoras durante su detención en la Subdirección Antiterrorista (SDAT). Bajo custodia policial, declaró que actuó "en nombre de Francia" cuando abrió fuego y mató a una persona e hirió a otras cinco en la localidad a las afueras de París. Los investigadores también hallaron en su domicilio una nota con nombres y números de teléfono de personalidades de izquierda. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: France 24

item.title: From bush food to biodegradable materials: Unlocking the potential of pigface
item.description: An Australian native plant traditionally used by Indigenous communities for food and medicine could help scientists develop stronger, more flexible biodegradable film. UNSW researchers have discovered that adding extracts from pigface, Carpobrotus glaucescens, a hardy coastal succulent, to seaweed-based films can significantly improve their strength and flexibility. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Electron beam tests advance safer sterilization method for flies that threaten livestock
item.description: Texas A&M AgriLife Research scientists have achieved early success using electron beam, or eBeam, technology for the sterile insect technique, or SIT, against New World screwworm flies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why teaching 'ethical' classroom use of AI to learn writing must include the right to refuse
item.description: What would it mean to teach students who are learning academic writing to use AI in "ethical" ways—for example, large language model (LLM) chatbots like ChatGPT, a specific form of GenAI? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Euclid offers best-ever 3D map of the universe to date
item.description: The Euclid Consortium and the European Space Agency (ESA) have released the first major batch of data from the Euclid space telescope. This release, which captures light from more than a billion objects and covers an area of sky equivalent to 9,500 full moons, lays the foundation for Europe's dark universe detective's largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos. Several German research facilities play crucial roles in the Euclid mission's success. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sea pigs from the abyss host unusual bacteria
item.description: In the deep ocean, translucent sea pigs trundle across the seafloor. Researchers at the University of Tokyo have discovered an unusual bacterium beneath the sea pig's "skin." Through fluorescent imaging, they determined the location of the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola. DNA analysis revealed a minimized genome of just 649,000 bases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI grading means university assessments could theoretically never be read by a human
item.description: There's a doomsday scenario where university students hand in work generated by artificial intelligence (AI), which is then graded by AI and university assessment no longer involves any humans at all. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ant colonies defy aging patterns as death risk falls and reproduction rises
item.description: Getting older usually brings a higher risk of death and declining reproduction. Yet for western harvester ant colonies, the opposite occurs. As a colony gets older, it becomes less likely to die and more likely to reproduce. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman
item.description: A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of this cosmic phenomenon and lays the groundwork for follow-up observations by the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Through NASA’s Lens: Capturing Space Shuttle Endeavour’s Move to LA
item.description: As a new exhibit opens showcasing NASA’s space shuttle Endeavour, NASA photographers look back at the final mission. These photographers documented the iconic images shared around the world on Sept. 21, 2012, while millions watched space shuttle Endeavour fly on top of the agency’s 747 Shuttle Carrier Aircraft for the last time. Endeavour’s new home […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Dede Dinius

item.title: Venezuela tells COP31 it has sovereign right to pump more oil
item.description: Venezuela’s Acting President ​Delcy Rodriguez’s comments at the UN ‌talks on Turkiye’s Mediterranean coast jar with efforts by other conference leaders to convince global governments to accelerate a ‌shift from carbon-emitting fossil fuels Fuente: The Hindu - International.

item.title: Light-controlled tool halts cellular recycling to offer disease mechanism clues
item.description: Inside each cell is a dynamic world of molecules and chemicals, signals and receivers, and construction and destruction. With all this activity, it's inevitable that cellular parts get worn down over time. Thankfully, cells have evolved an efficient recycling process that breaks old parts down to their building blocks, which can then be repurposed and reused. Christina Towers, Ph.D., is an expert on this recycling process, called autophagy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sunken treasure: Historic US ocean liner reborn as artificial reef
item.description: A majestic and all but indestructible 20th-century ocean liner that once ferried royal leaders, movie stars and even the "Mona Lisa" to the United States was being deliberately sunk Wednesday to become the world's largest artificial reef. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer
item.description: An NIH study found that women with high levels of two common “forever chemicals” had up to 93% higher rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The discovery raises concerns about the potential health effects of persistent chemicals found in everyday products. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: New way of detecting date-rape drug use found in Switzerland
item.description: Swiss researchers have found a new way of detecting the notorious date-rape drug GHB in urine for up to 72 hours after ingestion, in a possible boon to sexual assault investigations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Europe's Hera spacecraft begins close inspections of an asteroid rammed by NASA in a 2022 test
item.description: A European spacecraft has begun close inspections of an asteroid rammed by NASA four years ago in a planetary defense test. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Baboons made themselves at home in this town, and a battle between their defenders and haters ensued
item.description: The divisions over baboons run deep in Simon's Town, where their defenders and haters have clashed on social media and sometimes in real life for years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How potentials and electric fields together control reactions on catalyst surfaces
item.description: Researchers at the Interface Science Department (ISC) have shown that electrochemical reactions at solid-solution interfaces can be impacted by two closely related, yet, distinct factors. The applied potential can drive a reaction forward. Additionally, electric fields in the extended environment can modulate the ensembles that determine the activation parameters, without necessarily constituting a thermodynamic driving force themselves. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
item.description: Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from space. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 12 – Moon, Venus and Spica Meet
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 12 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Moon, Venus and […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scotland’s Flow Country
item.description: Blanket bogs in the Scottish Highlands store vast amounts of carbon. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
item.description: A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How war has connected the world for 500 years
item.description: With wars raging in Ukraine and across the Middle East, commentators increasingly ask whether we're sliding toward a third world war. But what makes a war "global"? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Indonesia fires burned through nearly 2.9 million hectares: Monitor
item.description: Fires in Indonesia driven partly by a strong El Niño have burned through 2.88 million hectares (7.1 million acres) so far in 2026, a monitor analyzing satellite imagery told AFP on Wednesday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
item.description: Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Only half of England's young workers outside higher education secure permanent contracts, down from 81%
item.description: The study of young people in England found that among those who did not progress to higher education, only 16% secured apprenticeships and just 23% had secured stable work by ages 19–20. Of those in work, only half had a permanent contract, down from 81% in a similar study six years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields
item.description: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has revealed a surprising secret hidden within the chaos of space: turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales. The discovery exposes an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Retired ocean liner to become largest artificial reef in the world
item.description: DESTIN, Fla. (AP) — An ocean liner that once was the fastest on the seas is headed to its final home on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico as the world’s largest artificial reef. Officials on Florida’s panhandle coast were scuttling the SS United States on Wednesday about 25 miles southwest of Destin, between […] Publicado también por: Mongabay. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5063-5069 Rocks and Chips
item.description: Written by William Farrand, Senior Research Scientist, Space Science Institute Earth planning date: Friday, Nov. 6, 2026 This week Curiosity has been completing its drill campaign at the “Nazca” drill hole. This is an area characterized by bedrock containing disk-shaped (or in a liberal interpretation, potato chip shaped … see linked image) crystal forms. A […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Microplastics found in wild mammals' blood more than 40 miles from human infrastructure
item.description: Animals, like humans, are taking up increasing amounts of tiny plastic particles. Such microplastics are demonstrably hazardous to many species under experimental conditions, and it is suspected that they may also pose a threat to animals in the wild. While data about microplastic concentrations in the terrestrial environment exist, it has not yet been clear if higher exposure also translates into higher microplastic accumulation in individual animals. A new paper published in Nature now confirms this link. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New study maps the genetic landscape of bovine TB across Wales
item.description: Bovine tuberculosis is evolving in different ways across different regions in Wales, according to the most detailed analysis of the bacterium conducted to date. One of the most significant animal health challenges facing Wales, bovine TB affects cattle health and farm businesses and places considerable emotional, social and financial pressures on farming communities. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Even parasites have parasites: Fungus infects powdery mildew
item.description: In the fungal kingdom, no one is safe from parasites—not even other parasites. A new study from North Carolina State University finds that Ampelomyces, an intracellular fungus that infects the plant disease powdery mildew, is far more common than previously known. By screening museum samples of powdery mildews up to about 150 years old, researchers discovered that not only is Ampelomyces quite common, but many specimens labeled as Ampelomyces are misidentified. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that walking, jogging, and even traditional weight training may be less effective at stimulating bone formation than high-intensity sports involving explosive movements and sudden changes in direction. Researchers found that activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, potentially revealing a better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Independent technique validates landmark M87* image
item.description: The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image was the work of hundreds of scientists and captured the first direct view of a black hole's shadow—becoming one of the most recognized scientific images of the modern era. A team of four from CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, has developed a powerful new imaging technique that validated the landmark 2019 image of the black hole at the center of galaxy M87. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This little brown mushroom is laced with a hallucinogen — and lethal toxins
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03639-2 A Florida fungus might combine the psychedelic compound psilocybin with deadly chemicals to defend itself against hungry animals. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Author Correction: SLAMF6 as a drug-targetable suppressor of T cell immunity against cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11409-3 Author Correction: SLAMF6 as a drug-targetable suppressor of T cell immunity against cancer Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: André Veillette

item.title: Massive atlas of brain region linked to a host of diseases is the most detailed yet
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03565-3 A global team profiled nearly 26 million brain cells from the basal ganglia to build a cross-species reference database that will help to understand conditions from Parkinson’s disease to addiction. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Miryam Naddaf

item.title: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks, overturning a long-standing theory about evolution. Rather than evolving to help animals turn their heads, necks may have emerged as part of the anatomical changes that allowed them to move using their front limbs. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Clean water, hidden risks: New technology reveals neurotoxicity missed by conventional water quality monitoring
item.description: A photograph of an orchestra can tell you whether the musicians are on stage and their instruments are intact. But it cannot tell you whether they are playing in harmony. Even when every musician is present, a subtle loss of coordination can change the entire performance. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fluorescent probes reveal fluid-like barriers inside nuclear pores of living human cells
item.description: Our genetic material is hidden inside the nucleus of our cells, well protected by a double membrane. All molecules wishing to pass through must thread their way through one of several thousand nuclear pores. The scaffold structure of these pores is well known. However, exactly how transport takes place within them has been the subject of much debate. Researchers at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU), the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics (MPI-BP) in Frankfurt am Main and Wuhan University in China have now shed light on the matter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Superconducting vortices provide experimental evidence that clogging is a phase transition
item.description: Clogging is a phenomenon in which moving particles get stuck, slowing or blocking the flow, but how this transition occurs has remained experimentally unproven. Researchers from Science Tokyo studied superconducting vortices to demonstrate that clogging is a nonequilibrium phase transition. Using a two-step measurement protocol, they distinguished clogging from conventional pinning and revealed that both transitions share a critical point, offering new insights into predicting and controlling clogging across diverse systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Looping DNA may help flowers grow nectar-producing organs
item.description: Nectaries are specialized floral tissues that secrete nectar to attract pollinators. Although the protein CRABS CLAW (CRC) is established as essential for nectary formation, the exact molecular mechanisms governing how it drives organ growth and secretion have remained unknown. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What is science? Even scientists can't agree
item.description: Scientists spend their careers trying to understand the world, but a new study suggests they have surprisingly different ideas about what science itself is. The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science even more than the general public does. Of the 18 descriptions of science examined, few received unqualified endorsement from scientists, who often expressed reservations even about ideas they generally agreed with. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Asteroid mining will crash the platinum market, but that's good news for Earth
item.description: Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question—what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A lingering blue glow and unexpected energy levels hint at new ways to control light in advanced materials
item.description: Scientists from the Physics Department and Organic Electroactive Materials research group at Durham University have made significant advances in understanding how materials absorb and release light in two recently published research papers in Nature Communications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find some of the 'very last wild and healthy ecosystems' in the world's oceans untouched by humans
item.description: Humans have left their mark on virtually every place on the planet, from the deep sea to the peaks of the highest mountains. But a few very remote atolls in the Pacific Ocean may be exceptions. A new Frontiers in Marine Science study has found two coral atolls, Bikar and Bokak, located on the territory of the Marshall Islands, to be some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region and perhaps the world. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Living with humility took on social weight in the late Middle Ages, historian argues
item.description: We're deep in the Middle Ages. In the mind's eye, monks stagger past, flagellating themselves to cleanse their sins and demonstrate their humility before God and creation. This was a time when humility—humilitas—was considered one of the fundamental virtues of Christian life. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More important than tropical cyclones: Scientists finally track the hidden weather systems behind most tropical rainfall
item.description: For the first time, researchers in Australia have identified and tracked the weather systems that are collectively more important to rainfall across the tropics than tropical cyclones. The work, published in the journal Weather and Climate Dynamics, has advanced a new way to investigate how tropical rain may change as the Earth warms up. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover uncounted right whale calf off Canada, bringing season's total to 24 amid population of 380
item.description: In a remarkable development, scientists have confirmed the sighting of a previously unrecorded North Atlantic right whale calf near Quebec, bringing this season's total to 24, the highest since 2009. Researchers believe the calf's mother, Silt, gave birth in the warmer waters of the southeastern U.S. Despite this positive news, the North Atlantic right whale population remains critically endangered, with an estimated 380 individuals. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: How pipes became status symbols in 18th-century Sweden
item.description: In the 18th century, a clay tobacco pipe could reveal more than you might think. Its length, quality and condition, as well as the way it was used, could signal social status. In a new doctoral thesis, Lund University archaeologist Robert Bergman Carter shows how smokeways at the time served as clear markers of status. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why holding on to loyal donors is not the right advice for every nonprofit
item.description: As humanitarian funding shrinks, conventional fundraising wisdom says to hold on to loyal donors. But new research shows that the value of a donor depends on how a nonprofit is set up. For many organizations, winning new donors matters more than keeping loyal ones. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why similar changes in cloud cover can have different climate effects
item.description: Marine low clouds over the world's eastern subtropical oceans strongly influence Earth's temperature by reflecting sunlight back to space. How these clouds change as the planet warms is one of the biggest uncertainties in predicting the severity of future warming. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deep-sea mollusk houses bacteria in tiny 'dragon balls,' revealing a new symbiotic structure
item.description: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have discovered a previously unknown specialized organelle structure in a deep-sea mollusk living at cold seeps in the South China Sea. Dedicated to maintaining bacterial symbiosis, this newly identified survival mechanism provides new insights into how deep-sea organisms adapt to nearly oxygen-free environments and opens new directions for research on chemosymbiosis, organelle evolution and deep-sea ecosystems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New method maps DNA folding and epigenetic marks in single cells
item.description: A new experimental procedure developed by researchers at Yale School of Medicine could help scientists better understand how DNA structure influences disease and development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When rain finally does come to drylands, only some microbes in the soil 'awaken'
item.description: In arid regions, the microbes that power threatened dryland soil ecosystems called biological soil crusts stay dormant over long periods, only "awakening" when they sense moisture from infrequent rainfall. Now, a team led by researchers at Penn State—driven by projections that those biocrusts will decline by as much as 40% in the next 45 years—found that when a dryland soil does get wet, most of the microbes in the biocrust stay inactive. It's a discovery that will inform ongoing efforts to conserve and restore biocrusts, according to the researchers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Biologists reveal chlorophyll-building enzyme's structure for first time and clarify its mechanism
item.description: Plants are green because of a pigment that is key to photosynthesis: chlorophyll. In its production, the enzyme chlorophyll synthase plays an important role. As part of an international collaboration, researchers from Osnabrück University, the Center Algatech in Třeboň and the University of Sheffield have now succeeded in deciphering the structure of this enzyme and gaining valuable insights into its mechanism. The findings are published in the journal Nature Chemical Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Biodegradable bubble moves away from lactic acid without a motor—a step toward artificial cells
item.description: A tiny biodegradable bubble can move away from a chemical on its own, without a motor. Living cells need complex molecular machinery to do this. This discovery by researchers led by chemist Daniela Wilson at Radboud University, together with colleagues at Durham University, is a step toward artificial cells with lifelike behavior and could, in the long term, provide an interesting approach for self-steering particles in targeted drug delivery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Setting timber ceilings on fire in the name safety and research
item.description: Queensland researchers are observing how fire spreads through ceiling compartments to aid the development of safer timber buildings. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Richards

item.title: Scientists challenge the dream of bringing extinct species back to life
item.description: Could extinction itself become a thing of the past? Advances in biotechnology, including ancient DNA sequencing, genome analysis and gene editing, have led some to believe that it may be possible to bring extinct species back to life. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chip identifies cells by their electrical signature, then separates them with a precisely aimed sound wave
item.description: In biomedicine, sorting cells accurately without damaging them remains a persistent problem. Current methods, like fluorescence-activated cell sorting, rely on labeling the cells extrinsically, which can stress the cells, alter their behavior and even interfere with the assay. A collaborative study between researchers in Singapore and China has now developed a noninvasive, label-free method to sort cells. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From remedy to prevention: Researchers call for proactive approach to protect the human right to water
item.description: More than 2 billion people, or approximately one-quarter of the world's population, lack access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene, according to the United Nations Children's Fund. Today, 16 years after the U.N. General Assembly recognized this access as a fundamental human right, its legal protection is well established, but the reality on the ground lags behind. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Symbolic clay figurines change our understanding of the prehistoric Middle East
item.description: Newly discovered artifacts are evidence of the earliest known example of a tradition of making clay figurines in the Middle East—and challenge long-held beliefs about when and how clay began to be used for symbolic purposes in the region, according to a study published in PLOS One by Laurent Davin from The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel, and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's secret weapon in the lunar space race may be ... procurement reform?
item.description: "The pace that's occurring, and the nature of the procurements, is unprecedented." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: Monkey foot and palm prints differ between individuals, as they do in humans
item.description: In three species of monkey, the complex pattern of ridges on the feet and palms varies between individuals, similar to human fingerprints, according to a study published in the open-access journal PLOS One by Juliana Vieira Flores Sales at Universidade de Brasília and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Misunderstandings about statistics common even among experienced researchers
item.description: Even researchers and people with extensive training in statistics often find it difficult to interpret statistical results correctly. This is shown by a new systematic review carried out by Uppsala University and others, in which researchers have analyzed 55 studies involving over 15,000 participants. The work is published in PLOS One. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Spain's massive stone tombs reveal collective burials continued well into Bronze Age
item.description: Iberian people continued using, and possibly building, massive necropolises well into the Bronze Age, according to a study published in PLOS One by Eduardo Vijande-Vila of the University of Cádiz, Spain, and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Frozen sperm enables embryo development in endangered Japanese bird for first time—but chick fails to hatch
item.description: The Okinawa rail (Hypotaenidia okinawae) is an endangered flightless bird endemic to the Yanbaru forest region of Okinawa Island in Japan. The bird has only recently begun recovering its numbers after introduced predators, such as the mongoose, and traffic accidents reduced its population to as low as 820 individuals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Overheating cattle: More and more dangerous heat is coming for northern Australia's herds
item.description: The Sunday roast and the backyard barbecue have long been Australian rituals. The country is one of the world's biggest consumers of red meat. The average Australian ate about 22 kilograms (49 pounds) of beef in 2024. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Jeff Bezos tiene una teoría sobre por qué la gente odia a los ricos: "El éxito no es sinónimo de maldad"
item.description: Probablemente preguntarle a un milmillonario porqué hay tanta gente enfadada con ellos y les ve como a los villanos de la película , sea parte del camino para encontrar una respuesta para un fenómeno que se ha intensificado en los últimos meses. Esa la pregunta que el entrevistador de la cadena Fox News, Bret Baier le formuló a nada menos que Jeff Bezos en el cuartel general de Blue Origin en Florida. Ver a la segunda mayor fortuna del mundo, con una fortuna estimada de 388.300 millones de dólares, respondiendo porqué los ricos no son los villanos y con cohetes espaciales de fondo es una… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Rubén Andrés

item.title: Excess reliance on AI could harm independent thinking in humanities education
item.description: The increasing use of content generated using artificial intelligence (AI) tools in university humanities classrooms is challenging what we think of as traditional academic integrity, intellectual responsibility and the authority of teachers, according to research in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient DNA reveals rare genetic condition behind a 1,600-year-old infant's single eye socket
item.description: Cyclopia is the most severe form of a rare birth condition in which the developing brain fails to divide into two separate halves. This can also affect facial development, sometimes leaving the baby with a single eye socket in the center of the forehead and severe facial abnormalities. Most babies born with this condition either die before or soon after birth. It is so rare that it occurs in roughly 1 in 100,000 births, so finding physical evidence of it from modern times is difficult, let alone from historical ones. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Acabamos de ver cómo un exoplaneta desaparece de la vista de nuestros telescopios. El culpable es su vecino invisible
item.description: Durante años, la astronomía ha consistido en mirar al cielo esperando a que las cosas pasen, y gracias a las misiones como Kepler o TESS, nos hemos acostumbrado a detectar exoplanetas observando su tránsito. Pero ante estas observaciones hay una pregunta bastante importante que ronda la cabeza: ¿qué pasa cuando un planeta al que llevas años observando puntualmente decide, de repente, desaparecer sin dejar rastro? Un ejemplo. Eso es exactamente lo que le ha ocurrido a TOI-2535 b , un exoplaneta del tamaño de Júpiter que ha protagonizado un "truco de magia" que antes no se había visto al… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: José A. Lizana

item.title: A double defense protects photosynthesis from extreme heat
item.description: Photosynthesis is fundamental to life on Earth, allowing plants and microalgae to convert sunlight and carbon dioxide into organic compounds. However, this essential process is highly vulnerable to heat. As global temperatures rise and heat waves become more frequent, declining photosynthetic efficiency threatens agricultural productivity and the large-scale cultivation of microalgae for biofuels and other valuable products. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3D protein complex model sheds light on barley grain dormancy
item.description: Researchers from Adelaide University and Plant Synthetic Biology Australia have uncovered new insights into the molecular machinery controlling the dormancy-to-germination transition in barley, potentially paving the way for improved crop varieties and better outcomes for farmers, maltsters and brewers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Taking into account the role of neglected farmer groups in recharging groundwater
item.description: A new study by researchers at the Indo-French Cell for Water Sciences (IFCWS), Indian Institute of Science (IISc), introduces a new framework for water budgeting in agricultural regions that includes farmers' social categories that are usually neglected. The work is published in the Journal of Hydrology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Centaurus A in the spotlight: Plasma simulations reproduce black hole jets' mysterious bright edges
item.description: Around 12 million light-years away, the supermassive black hole of the galaxy Centaurus A is hurling two enormous plasma jets into space at nearly the speed of light. These so-called jets are brighter at their edges than at their center. The reason for this was previously unclear but has now been explained by a team from the Chair of Astronomy at the University of Würzburg. The research is published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Genetic study describes two new species of Amazonian howler monkeys
item.description: A sweeping genetic study of howler monkeys has revealed two previously unrecognized species in the Amazon, identified a potentially distinct species in the Caribbean and prompted researchers to reconsider how several populations are classified. The new study examined genetic relationships across the genus Alouatta, using genomic data, physical characteristics and museum specimens. Researchers formally described […] Fuente: Mongabay.
item.dc:creator: Xavier Bartaburu

item.title: Argon on Uranus and Neptune may reveal more about their origins than their interiors
item.description: Measurements of an argon isotope could help scientists understand whether the interiors of Uranus and Neptune, our solar system's so-called ice giants, are dominated by ice or rock. New research led by Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) and published in The Planetary Science Journal measured the planets' atmospheric argon-40 to estimate the amount of rock found beneath their surfaces and search for clues about the planets' origins, including where and how they formed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: COP31 leaders urge focus on climate action despite global conflicts
item.description: Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are seeking agreement at COP31 on a proposal from Turkey to increase the share of electricity in global ‌energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels Fuente: The Hindu - International.

item.title: Why some dinosaurs get all the attention and others don't
item.description: If you ask anyone to name a dinosaur, there's a good chance they'll say Tyrannosaurus rex, that fearsome prehistoric predator with its enormous jaws and razor-sharp teeth. But what about a lesser-known dinosaur such as Iguanodon or Plateosaurus? Probably not. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A gold–copper strategy for building interlocked nitrogen-doped carbon nanohoops
item.description: Catenanes are molecules in which two or more rings are mechanically interlocked like the links of a chain, without any chemical bonds between them. Since Jean-Pierre Sauvage, who later shared the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, reported an efficient metal-templated synthesis in 1983, catenanes have attracted attention as fundamental frameworks for molecular machines. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: About 15,000 land vertebrate species could lose habitat to sea-level rise by 2100
item.description: The rate of sea-level rise is now more than 4 millimeters (0.16 inches) per year, having more than doubled since 1993–2002. Scientists estimate that this figure may go up to 10 millimeters (0.39 inches) per year in the near future. The inundation of coastlines and islands will affect human and animal habitats alike. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Por primera vez, un robot ha construido de forma autónoma parte de una estructura en el espacio
item.description: Para estudiar el espacio profundo y detectar incluso los objetos más débiles necesitaremos telescopios espaciales cada vez más grandes . Si queremos comunicarnos de forma más eficiente en el espacio, son necesarias antenas de transmisión mucho mayores que las que se usan hoy en día. El problema es que ambas soluciones chocan con un mismo obstáculo: su tamaño. Hoy en día, los cohetes espaciales tienen un límite de carga que no permite poner en órbita dispositivos colosales. Hay algunas soluciones, pero también están bastante limitadas. Por eso, un equipo de científicos de Caltech ha probado un… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Bennu asteroid analysis suggests unexpected origins for organics in space
item.description: Samples from the Bennu asteroid, which is currently more than 200 million miles (322 million kilometers) from Earth, and the Murchison meteorite, which fell to Earth in 1969, both contain molecules that build proteins necessary for life. New research has found that the molecules may have formed through the same process but originated far from one another in the solar system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Measles is surging in the U.S. — and outbreaks can cost millions
item.description: A new tool developed by Johns Hopkins researchers estimates that the 2025 measles outbreak in the U.S. carried an economic cost of more than $37 million. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: New strategy boosts iron-based single-atom catalysts for Fenton-like reactions
item.description: Researchers at the Xinjiang Technical Institute of Physics and Chemistry (XTIPC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) have developed a core-shell confined iron-based single-atom catalyst that combines high Fenton-like catalytic activity with structural stability, enabling nearly complete removal of 2,4-dichlorophenol (2,4-DCP) within 20 minutes under mildly acidic conditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The faces of iridium: One metal, many reactions
item.description: The same metal can have many faces, and each tells a different chemical story. At the atomic scale, those different faces can push the same reaction along very different paths. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Italia: 20 explosiones en cuatro meses ponen a Roma en alerta; temen guerra entre clanes criminales
item.description: En los últimos meses, Roma ha registrado una ola de explosiones que mantiene en alerta a las autoridades. Cerca de una veintena de artefactos han causado daños en comercios y zonas residenciales, mientras investigadores y organismos antimafia analizan una posible disputa entre clanes criminales por el control del narcotráfico y del territorio. La Policía ha reforzado los operativos para evitar una escalada de violencia y contener un conflicto que podría extenderse.Un informe de Irene Savio con cámara de Esma Cakir. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: III-nitride device integrates sensing and memory for in-sensor computing
item.description: A new study published in Nature Materials reports that researchers have developed an aluminum gallium nitride device that combines light detection, memory and basic processing by controlling charge at polarization interfaces. The device can detect light at the nanowatt-per-square-centimeter level and operate stably at temperatures up to 300°C. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A standard shortcut, used since the 1970s, hides a magneto-optic effect in ordinary glass fiber
item.description: For more than 50 years, engineers have described light in optical fiber using a convenient shortcut, one that works so well it is rarely questioned. Engineers at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg, South Africa, have now shown that this shortcut hides a small but real effect. A magnet placed beside a multimode fiber, rather than along it, can change the light traveling inside. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New algorithm improves phase readout for space-based gravitational wave detection
item.description: In a study published in Optics Communications, a research group led by Yu Tao from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics (CIOMP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences proposed a new analytical phase readout algorithm for deep frequency modulation interferometry (DFMI). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
item.description: A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Wonder and ore: A spectacular new view from space maps Australia's mineral wealth
item.description: A new tool that uses detailed satellite images to help unlock Australia's mineral wealth has been unveiled. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
item.description: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
